findings.issue: L1 is presented as sufficient for a solo project, but its mandatory development loop requires two fresh-context audits, a cross-runtime second opinion, and cross-review. Codex may participate only through L2 seats. Therefore an L1-only consumer cannot conform to L1, and the tiers are not independently adoptable as claimed.
findings.suggestion: Define explicit conformance profiles. Keep a genuinely single-session L1 baseline, move cross-session/cross-runtime requirements into an L2 assurance profile, and specify permitted substitutes when only one runtime is available.

findings.issue: “Every file belongs to exactly one layer” conflicts with AGENTS.md files containing both layer-tagged A and B content and framework-owned forge regions inside project-owned files. Copier path controls such as _skip_if_exists and _exclude cannot enforce ownership or safely update marked regions within a shared file.
findings.suggestion: Separate A and B source files and generate runtime-facing composite files, or define a formal region-ownership manifest, deterministic composer, conflict policy, and update conformance tests.

findings.issue: “One append = record + transport” is load-bearing but has no defined atomicity, ordering, delivery, acknowledgement, retry, deduplication, cursor, or crash-recovery semantics. Postgres, SQLite, and JSONL cannot be treated as interchangeable without a semantic contract; doorbell retries can otherwise duplicate or lose work.
findings.suggestion: Define a canonical event-log protocol with stable event IDs, per-stream ordering, idempotent writes, consumer offsets, explicit at-least-once delivery, transaction boundaries, and recovery behavior. Require every backend to pass the same conformance suite and document weaker degraded-mode guarantees.

findings.issue: Importing root AGENTS.md from root CLAUDE.md does not itself specify how directory-dependent nested AGENTS.md files reach Claude sessions. More generally, native AGENTS.md discovery, precedence, import expansion, and nested-file behavior are asserted across several tools without a versioned capability contract.
findings.suggestion: Implement a runtime-specific context compiler/resolver with an exact precedence algorithm and compatibility tests. Generate native per-directory entry files where a runtime cannot reproduce the canonical hierarchy.

findings.issue: CI cannot calculate the stated worst-case payload while the payload includes uncontrolled user-level files, runtime-specific extras, imports, and potentially different resolver behavior. A Codex byte ceiling also does not establish a safe budget for every other runtime.
findings.suggestion: Budget only deterministic repository-owned compiled payloads, report external/global context separately, define byte-counting and import-expansion rules, and maintain tested per-runtime limits with reserved headroom.

findings.issue: A persistent, revivable session-handle is assumed, but no capability contract exists for runtimes that cannot reliably resume, address, or externally re-invoke a session. Heartbeat, watchdog, pacemaker, and doorbell races can also revive the same seat twice and create split-brain workers.
findings.suggestion: Specify a seat state machine with leases, fencing tokens, generation numbers, ownership transfer, terminal states, lost-handle recovery, and runtime capability negotiation. Define non-revivable runtimes as an explicit supported mode.

findings.issue: Adding project_namespace fields is insufficient to support a second consumer safely. Namespace issuance, uniqueness, authorization, PostgREST RLS, cross-project query prevention, retention, quotas, schema versions, and migrations are undefined.
findings.suggestion: Make tenant isolation part of the backend contract: immutable project IDs, compound keys, authorization rules, migration/version tables, namespace lifecycle, retention policy, and adversarial isolation tests.

findings.issue: The architecture alternates between cumulative adoption (“a fleet adds L2”) and independent adoption. L2 uses L1 concepts and policies, while L3 assumes seats, worktrees, and runtime configuration but is also declared independently adoptable.
findings.suggestion: Publish a dependency DAG and distinguish independently testable components from independently deployable profiles. State the minimum required components and supported combinations for solo, fleet, and isolated-fleet operation.

findings.issue: none, schema, compose, and branch provide materially different isolation guarantees, but there is no common lifecycle contract for provisioning, migrations, seeding, connection injection, cleanup, crash recovery, or collision detection. Port allocation has similarly unspecified ownership and reclamation semantics.
findings.suggestion: Define an isolation-adapter interface and state machine with capability levels, unique allocation leases, readiness checks, cleanup guarantees, secret handling, and recovery tests. Avoid presenting weaker adapters as equivalent isolation.

findings.issue: Runner-originated evidence is not necessarily current or relevant. The architecture does not bind evidence to a commit/tree hash, worktree, command definition, test selection, environment, or gate version, so stale or unrelated results can satisfy a gate. RED also needs proof that failure was expected rather than an infrastructure error.
findings.suggestion: Define append-only evidence events with provenance and content hashes, freshness/invalidation rules, concurrency handling, expected-failure classification, and gate-specific predicates evaluated against the exact candidate revision.

findings.issue: Local missing or malformed state may only warn and never block, while hard failure is limited to CI inputs that are versioned. The document does not identify which authoritative evidence is versioned or how local runner evidence reaches CI. This can reduce mandatory stages to warnings and contradict “enforce, don’t suggest.”
findings.suggestion: Classify every gate input by authority and persistence. Define how evidence is transported to CI, make unavailable evidence distinct from passing evidence, and require the authoritative merge gate to fail closed without valid inputs.

findings.issue: The source of truth for the model matrix is unclear: it is described as generated configuration, derived from a questionnaire, and modified by per-project overrides. The same law also categorizes rosters with generated indexes even though rosters are mutable runtime state and unsuitable for regenerate-plus-git-diff checks.
findings.suggestion: Define separate categories for authored source, generated artifact, runtime state, and derived view. Specify precedence and merge rules for questionnaire answers and overrides, prohibit edits to generated outputs, and apply CI freshness checks only to deterministic versioned artifacts.

findings.issue: Additive migration protects a live project during rollout but does not define long-term compatibility for Copier updates, hub schemas, event formats, chain state, generated files, or runtime adapters. _skip_if_exists can also permanently strand consumers on obsolete framework-owned files.
findings.suggestion: Add semantic versions, compatibility ranges, schema and state migrations, deprecation windows, generated-file ownership metadata, upgrade tests from supported prior versions, and an explicit conflict-resolution workflow for Copier updates.

findings.issue: “Seats never read another seat’s mailbox” is stated as protocol etiquette, not an enforceable authorization rule. Generic reads such as open and blocked may expose messages or project data, especially through the shared PostgREST backend.
findings.suggestion: Define the mailbox data model, visibility rules, sender/recipient identities, authentication, backend-enforced authorization, administrative repair privileges, and equivalent behavior for local backends.

findings.issue: A “bounded watcher” and event-triggered re-invocation are not sufficiently specified for missed-event races, event bursts, backpressure, coalescing, watcher expiry, reconnect cursors, or runtimes lacking a safe external resume interface.
findings.suggestion: Specify subscribe-from-cursor behavior, durable wake intent, debounce/coalescing policy, resource bounds, retries, authentication, and the polling fallback’s correctness guarantees.

findings.issue: Hooks, launchers, per-worktree trust configuration, shared hub access, and override tokens create a substantial execution and credential boundary, but there is no threat model. A generated project could leak secrets through evidence, hub records, logs, or malicious hook changes.
findings.suggestion: Define trust boundaries, least-privilege credentials, secret redaction, hook integrity checks, untrusted-PR behavior, override-token issuance and expiry, audit retention, and CI restrictions before treating the enforcement system as portable.

findings.issue: The framework supplies gate patterns and a generated CI skeleton while the consumer owns the pipeline, leaving it unclear which integration points are normative and what constitutes a conforming implementation on another CI provider.
findings.suggestion: Define a provider-neutral gate contract with required commands, inputs, outputs, exit semantics, and artifact handling; treat provider-specific skeletons as tested adapters.

strongest_aspect: The architecture derives concrete design laws from observed failure modes and separates single-session method, cross-session coordination, and collision isolation more coherently than the former eight-layer taxonomy.
biggest_risk: The portable surface depends on unproven equivalence across runtime context resolution, resumable sessions, and three very different hub backends. Without executable capability and conformance contracts, the second consuming project will expose divergent behavior, lost or duplicated coordination events, and unsafe template-update ownership.
